sections.title: 1. Bond Fundamentals: Structure, Pricing, and Yield
sections.overview: Debt securities are loans from investors to issuers in which the issuer promises to pay periodic interest (coupon) and return principal (par) at maturity. The SIE tests fluency in par value, coupon rate, market price quoting conventions, and the inverse relationship between bond prices and prevailing interest rates.
key_concepts: Par (face) value: standard $1,000 for corporates and most municipals; $100 for Treasuries (quoted) and $5,000 minimum denomination for most munis.
Coupon (nominal/stated) rate: fixed annual interest as a percentage of par; typically paid semiannually.

Quoting: corporate and muni bonds quoted as a percentage of par in 1/8ths (e.g., 98 1/2 = $985); Treasury notes/bonds quoted in 32nds (e.g., 98.16 = 98 + 16/32 = $985.00 on $1,000 par); T-bills quoted on a discount yield basis.
Inverse price/yield relationship: when interest rates rise, outstanding bond prices fall; when rates fall, bond prices rise.
Discount bond: price < par (market yield > coupon). Premium bond: price > par (market yield < coupon). Par bond: price = par (market yield = coupon).
Yield hierarchy on a DISCOUNT bond (lowest to highest): Nominal < Current Yield < YTM < YTC.
Yield hierarchy on a PREMIUM bond (highest to lowest): Nominal > Current Yield > YTM > YTC.
Accrued interest: buyer pays seller interest accrued from last coupon date up to but NOT including settlement date.
Day-count conventions: Corporate and municipal bonds use 30/360 (each month = 30 days, year = 360). Treasury notes/bonds use actual/actual.
Bond indenture (Trust Indenture Act of 1939): contract specifying terms, covenants, trustee duties — required for corporate issues > $50 million.
Credit rating agencies (NRSROs): Moody's, S&P, Fitch. Investment grade: S&P/Fitch BBB- and above; Moody's Baa3 and above. Below = high-yield/junk/speculative.
Callable bonds: issuer can redeem early — favors issuer when rates fall; investors demand higher coupon and face call risk.
Putable bonds: holder can force redemption — favors investor when rates rise.
Convertible bonds: bondholder can exchange for issuer's common stock at a stated conversion ratio; typically lower coupon.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §2.1.2 — Debt instruments: knowledge of par, coupon, yield, ratings, callable/convertible features, varying maturities, price/rate relationship.
FINRA SIE Outline §2.2 — Risks include interest rate, credit, inflation/purchasing power, liquidity, reinvestment, prepayment.
formulas: Annual Coupon ($) = Coupon Rate × Par Value
Current Yield = Annual Coupon / Current Market Price
Conversion Ratio = Par Value / Conversion Price
Parity Price of Bond = Market Price of Stock × Conversion Ratio
Parity Price of Stock = Market Price of Bond / Conversion Ratio
Bond Price Quote (corp/muni): Quote × 10 = Dollar Price (e.g., 95.5 → $955)
mnemonics: ICE on discount bonds: yields Increase Coupon-to-Call as price decreases — Nominal, Current, YTM, YTC (ascending).
Premium = MIRROR: yields go DOWN — Nominal, Current, YTM, YTC (descending).
Bond seesaw: 'Prices and rates ride a seesaw — opposite ends.'

sections.title: 2. Yield Measures: Nominal, Current, YTM, YTC
sections.overview: Four standard yield measures express return differently. Knowing which yield to compare under what conditions (and how call/premium/discount affects the ranking) is heavily tested.
key_concepts: Nominal yield (coupon rate): fixed at issuance; relevant only to par.
Current yield: cash income return on present market price; ignores capital gain/loss and time to maturity.
Yield to Maturity (YTM): internal rate of return assuming the bond is held to maturity and all coupons reinvested at the YTM; reflects coupon, price, and time.
Yield to Call (YTC): IRR assuming bond is called on first/specified call date; most meaningful on premium callable bonds.
Yield to Worst (YTW): lowest of YTM and all possible YTCs; the conservative measure quoted to investors on callable premium bonds.
Reinvestment risk: actual realized yield deviates from YTM if coupons are reinvested at rates other than YTM.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §2.1.2 — Yield concepts including callable and convertible features.
formulas: Current Yield = Annual Coupon / Market Price
Approximate YTM = [Annual Coupon + (Par − Price)/Years to Maturity] / [(Par + Price)/2]
Approximate YTC = [Annual Coupon + (Call Price − Price)/Years to Call] / [(Call Price + Price)/2]
mnemonics: 'Call the Premium, Mature the Discount' — quote YTC on premium callable bonds; YTM is usually worst on discount bonds.

sections.title: 3. U.S. Treasury Securities
sections.overview: Direct obligations of the U.S. government — considered free of credit (default) risk. Interest is exempt from state and local tax but subject to federal tax. Settlement is T+1 (always has been).
key_concepts: Treasury Bills (T-bills): maturities 4, 8, 13, 17, 26, 52 weeks; issued at a discount, redeemed at par; no coupon; sold via weekly competitive/non-competitive auction.
Treasury Notes (T-notes): maturities 2, 3, 5, 7, 10 years; semiannual coupon; quoted in 32nds.
Treasury Bonds (T-bonds): maturities 20 and 30 years; semiannual coupon; quoted in 32nds.
TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities): principal adjusts semiannually with CPI; fixed coupon rate paid on adjusted principal. Protects against inflation/purchasing-power risk.
STRIPS: zero-coupon Treasuries created by stripping coupons from notes/bonds. Investor accretes 'phantom income' annually — taxable federally each year even though no cash received.
Treasury Receipts: zero-coupon instruments issued by broker-dealers (not direct U.S. obligations); backed by Treasuries held in escrow.
Auction process: competitive bids (specify yield) and non-competitive bids (accept stop-out yield, max $10 million per auction). Non-competitive filled first.
Quoted as percentage of par in 32nds (T-notes/bonds); T-bills quoted on annualized discount yield basis.
Settlement: T+1 (regular way for Treasuries — historically and currently).
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §2.1.2 — Treasury securities (bills, notes, receipts, bonds).
formulas: T-bill Discount Yield = [(Par − Price)/Par] × (360/Days to Maturity)
TIPS Adjusted Principal = Original Principal × (Current CPI / Reference CPI)
TIPS Coupon Payment = Fixed Coupon Rate × Adjusted Principal / 2
mnemonics: 'BiNoBo' — Bills (≤1 yr), Notes (2–10 yr), Bonds (20–30 yr).
STRIPS = Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal Securities — 'phantom income.'

sections.title: 4. U.S. Agency and Mortgage-Backed Securities
sections.overview: Agency debt is issued by federal agencies or government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs). Only Ginnie Mae carries the full faith and credit of the U.S. government; GSEs carry only an implied backing. MBS pass through principal and interest from underlying mortgages and carry prepayment and extension risk.
key_concepts: GNMA (Ginnie Mae): direct U.S. government agency — only agency with full faith and credit guarantee. Issues MBS backed by FHA/VA mortgages.
FNMA (Fannie Mae) and FHLMC (Freddie Mac): GSEs — publicly traded; NOT direct U.S. obligations. Purchase conforming mortgages from lenders and securitize.
Pass-through MBS: monthly payments of interest AND principal flow through to investor.
Prepayment risk: borrowers refinance when rates fall — investor receives principal back early and must reinvest at lower rates.
Extension risk: when rates rise, prepayments slow, lengthening duration when investor would prefer shorter.

CMOs (Collateralized Mortgage Obligations): MBS divided into tranches with different maturities and prepayment priorities. PAC (Planned Amortization Class) tranches have most predictable cash flows; Z-tranches (accrual) receive no payments until earlier tranches are retired.
CMO interest taxed at federal, state, and local levels (unlike Treasuries).
Asset-Backed Securities (ABS): backed by non-mortgage receivables (credit cards, auto loans, student loans). Standard ABS settle T+1.
Settlement of MBS/TBAs governed by SIFMA's separate TBA schedule.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §2.1.2 — Agency securities including ABS and MBS.
mnemonics: 'GNMA = Government, Guaranteed.' FNMA/FHLMC = GSEs (implied only).
PAC = Predictable; Z = Zero payments until later.

sections.title: 5. Corporate Bonds
sections.overview: Corporate debt is taxable at all levels and ranges from senior secured to deeply subordinated. The SIE tests the liquidation order, secured vs. unsecured categories, and special structures (convertibles, zero-coupon, high-yield).
key_concepts: Secured bonds (collateralized): Mortgage bonds (real property), Equipment trust certificates (rolling stock — airlines/railroads), Collateral trust bonds (securities of other companies pledged).

Unsecured bonds: Debentures (backed by issuer's full faith/credit only), Subordinated debentures (junior to other debentures), Income (adjustment) bonds (pay interest only if earned — used in reorganization), Guaranteed bonds (third-party guarantee).

Liquidation order (priority of claims): (1) Secured creditors → (2) Unsecured creditors and general creditors (incl. debentures) → (3) Subordinated debt → (4) Preferred stockholders → (5) Common stockholders.
Wage/tax claims and administrative expenses of bankruptcy paid before general unsecured creditors.
Convertible bonds: lower coupon, allow exchange into common stock at fixed conversion ratio.
Zero-coupon corporates: issued at deep discount; no current cash interest; phantom income taxed annually.
High-yield (junk) bonds: rated below BBB-/Baa3; speculative; higher default risk.
Settlement: corporate bonds settle T+1 with 30/360 accrued interest.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §2.1.2 — Corporate bonds.
Rule 2262 — Disclosure of control relationship between member and issuer required before customer transaction.
formulas: Accrued Interest (corp) = Coupon × (Days from last interest payment to settlement, 30/360) / 360
mnemonics: Liquidation order: 'Secured, Unsecured, Subordinated, Preferred, Common' — 'Some Unsecured Suckers Pay Common.'
'METC' secured types: Mortgage, Equipment trust, Trust (collateral).

sections.title: 6. Municipal Securities
sections.overview: Munis are debt issued by states, local governments, and their political subdivisions. Interest is generally exempt from federal income tax and, if the holder lives in the issuing state, often exempt from state/local tax as well ('triple tax-exempt'). Two principal categories: General Obligation (GO) and Revenue bonds.
key_concepts: General Obligation (GO) bonds: backed by issuer's full faith, credit, and taxing power. State GOs backed by income/sales tax; local GOs backed by ad valorem (property) tax. Often require voter approval; subject to statutory debt limits.

Revenue bonds: backed by income from a specific project/facility (toll road, airport, water/sewer, hospital, stadium). No taxing power pledge; no voter approval required; no statutory debt limit. Generally higher yield than GOs.
Feasibility study required for revenue bonds — projects expected revenues vs. debt service.
Revenue bond covenants: rate covenant (set rates sufficient to cover debt service), maintenance covenant, insurance covenant, additional bonds test.
Flow of funds (net revenue pledge typical order): Operations & maintenance → Debt service → Debt service reserve → Reserve maintenance → Renewal/replacement → Surplus.
Special tax bonds: backed by a specific excise tax (gasoline, tobacco, alcohol).
Special assessment bonds: paid by those who directly benefit (e.g., new sidewalks, sewers).
Moral obligation bonds: state legislature may (not must) appropriate funds to cover deficiencies.
Industrial Development Revenue Bonds (IDRs/IDBs): issued by municipality, proceeds used by a private corporation that is the actual obligor. Often AMT-subject.
Build America Bonds (BABs): taxable munis (legacy program); issuer or holder received federal subsidy.

Bond Anticipation Notes (BANs), Tax Anticipation Notes (TANs), Revenue Anticipation Notes (RANs), TRANs, Construction Loan Notes (CLNs): short-term muni notes rated MIG 1–3 by Moody's (best to lowest IG).
Variable-rate demand obligations (VRDOs): floating-rate long-term munis with put feature.
Settlement: municipal bonds settle T+1 (MSRB Rules G-12 and G-15, effective 5/28/2024); 30/360 accrued interest convention unchanged.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §2.1.2 — Municipal securities (GO, revenue, special types, taxable munis, short-term obligations).
Rule G-17 — Fair dealing: municipal securities dealers must deal fairly with all persons and not engage in deceptive practices.
Rule G-30 — Prevailing market price/markup standards on municipal transactions; 'waterfall' analysis for PMP.
Rule D-12 — Defines 'Municipal Fund Security' — issued by an issuer that would be an investment company but for ICA §2(b) (e.g., 529 plans, LGIPs).
formulas: Tax-Equivalent Yield (TEY) = Tax-Exempt Yield / (1 − Investor's Marginal Federal Tax Rate)
Net Yield After Tax (on taxable) = Taxable Yield × (1 − Tax Rate)
Accrued Interest (muni) = Coupon × (Days, 30/360) / 360
mnemonics: GO = Government's Obligation (taxing power). Revenue = Revenue from a project.
Muni note ratings — MIG 1 best, MIG 3 lowest IG.
Anticipation notes: 'BTRT C' — BAN, TAN, RAN, TRAN, CLN.

sections.title: 7. Money Market Instruments
sections.overview: Money market instruments are short-term (≤ 1 year), highly liquid debt securities. They are used by issuers for short-term funding and by investors as cash-equivalents.
key_concepts: Treasury bills: short-term U.S. obligations, sold at discount, max 52 weeks.
Commercial paper: unsecured corporate promissory notes; maximum maturity 270 days to qualify for §3(a)(3) exemption from registration under the Securities Act of 1933. Issued at a discount.

Negotiable (Jumbo) CDs: bank-issued, minimum $100,000 (commonly $1 million+); transferable in secondary market; only the first $250,000 per depositor per insured bank per ownership category is FDIC-insured.
Bankers' Acceptances (BAs): time drafts drawn on a bank, used to finance international trade; maximum 270 days; sold at discount.
Repurchase Agreements (Repos): sale of securities with agreement to repurchase at a higher price — effectively a collateralized loan.
Federal Funds: overnight loans of reserves between member banks; rate set by market (target band by FOMC).
Eurodollars: U.S. dollar deposits held outside U.S.; Eurodollar bonds issued outside U.S.
LIBOR was permanently discontinued 6/30/2023 and replaced by SOFR (Secured Overnight Financing Rate) as the USD floating-rate benchmark.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §2.1.2 — Money market instruments, CDs, bankers' acceptances, commercial paper.
Securities Act of 1933 §3(a)(3) — exemption for commercial paper with maturity ≤ 270 days.
formulas: Discount Yield = [(Par − Price)/Par] × (360/Days)
Bond-Equivalent Yield = [(Par − Price)/Price] × (365/Days)
mnemonics: Money market 'CD-BA-CP-Repo-FF-T-bill' — six core instruments.
Commercial paper: 'CP270' = 270-day max.
FDIC: $250K per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.

sections.title: 8. Taxation of Bond Interest
sections.overview: Tax treatment of interest differs by issuer type. The SIE expects fluency in the federal/state/local matrix and the tax-equivalent yield comparison.
key_concepts: U.S. Treasury interest: TAXABLE federally; EXEMPT from state and local tax.
Federal agency interest (FNMA, FHLMC, GNMA, CMOs): taxable at federal, state, and local levels.
Corporate bond interest: taxable at all levels (federal, state, local).

Municipal bond interest: EXEMPT from federal tax; exempt from state/local if investor resides in issuing state ('triple tax-exempt' includes territories: Puerto Rico, Guam, USVI — exempt nationally regardless of residence).
Taxable munis (BABs, certain private activity): taxable federally.
Private Activity Bonds (PABs): interest may be subject to Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT).
Original Issue Discount (OID): on Treasury STRIPS/zeros, accreted annually as taxable interest ('phantom income'); cost basis steps up annually.
Market discount: accrued portion taxed as ordinary income at sale/maturity.
Bond premium amortization: required for tax-exempt munis (reduces basis); elective for taxable bonds.
Capital gains: difference between sale price and adjusted basis (after OID accretion or premium amortization) — taxed at capital gains rates.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §2.1.2 — Generate income (interest).
formulas: Tax-Equivalent Yield = Municipal Yield / (1 − Federal Marginal Tax Rate)
For investor in state with state tax exemption: TEY = Muni Yield / [1 − (Fed + State Marginal Rates)]
After-Tax Yield on Taxable = Taxable Yield × (1 − Marginal Tax Rate)
mnemonics: Treasury = 'Fed Yes, State No.'
Muni = 'Fed No, State Maybe (Yes if in-state).'
Corporate/Agency = 'Tax everywhere.'

sections.title: 9. Issuance and Underwriting of Debt
sections.overview: Debt securities are brought to market via competitive bid, negotiated underwriting, or (for Treasuries) auction. The structure of the syndicate and the mechanics of the offering differ between corporate, municipal, and government issues.
key_concepts: Competitive bid: issuer publishes a Notice of Sale; underwriting syndicates submit sealed bids; lowest net interest cost (NIC) or true interest cost (TIC) wins. Common for GO munis.
Negotiated offering: issuer selects underwriter directly and negotiates terms. Common for revenue bonds and corporate bonds.
Treasury auction: weekly/monthly; competitive bidders specify yield, non-competitive accept stop-out (max $10MM/auction). Single-price (Dutch) auction.
Syndicate: group of underwriters formed to spread risk and distribute the issue. Lead/senior manager runs the books.
Underwriting spread: difference between price paid to issuer and offering price. Components: manager's fee, underwriting fee, concession (to selling group/syndicate member), takedown.
Bond ratings used for marketing; ratings agencies are NRSROs (Moody's, S&P, Fitch).
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §2.1.2 — Negotiated vs. competitive offerings; auction.
formulas: Total Takedown = Additional Takedown + Concession
Underwriting Spread = Manager's Fee + Underwriting Fee + Total Takedown
mnemonics: Bond underwriting compensation 'MUC-T': Manager's fee, Underwriting fee, Concession, Takedown.
'GO Competitive, Revenue Negotiated' — typical bond offering method by type.

sections.title: 10. Debt-Specific Risks
sections.overview: Bond investors face risks beyond ordinary market risk — particularly interest rate risk, credit risk, reinvestment risk, call risk, prepayment risk, and inflation risk. The SIE tests identification of each and how various securities expose investors differently.
key_concepts: Interest rate risk: risk of bond prices falling when rates rise. Greatest for long-duration, low-coupon bonds. Zero-coupon and long-maturity bonds are most rate-sensitive.
Credit (default) risk: risk that issuer fails to pay interest/principal. Highest for low-rated/junk bonds; lowest for Treasuries.
Reinvestment risk: risk that coupon payments must be reinvested at lower prevailing rates. Zero-coupon bonds eliminate reinvestment risk (no coupons to reinvest).
Call risk: risk that callable bonds will be called when rates drop, forcing reinvestment at lower yields.
Prepayment risk: borrowers prepay mortgages when rates fall — affects MBS/CMO holders.
Extension risk: opposite of prepayment — slower prepayments lengthen duration when rates rise.
Inflation/purchasing power risk: fixed income loses real value as inflation rises. TIPS mitigate this.
Liquidity (marketability) risk: difficulty selling at fair price; greatest for thinly traded munis, low-rated corporates.
Currency risk: foreign-denominated bonds — exchange-rate fluctuation.
Political/legislative risk: changes in tax law (e.g., loss of municipal tax exemption) or sovereign policy.
Capital risk: risk of losing principal — present in all but the safest securities.
Systematic (market) risk vs. non-systematic (issuer-specific) risk — non-systematic mitigated by diversification.
rules: FINRA SIE Outline §2.2 — Risk types and mitigation (diversification, rebalancing, hedging).
Rule 2261 — Member must disclose financial condition to bona fide customer on request.
formulas: Real Return ≈ Nominal Return − Inflation Rate
mnemonics: Bond risks: 'CCC-LIP-RP' — Credit, Call, Currency, Liquidity, Inflation, Political, Reinvestment, Prepayment.
'Zeros: no reinvestment risk; max interest-rate risk.'
Long maturity + low coupon = highest interest rate sensitivity.

sections.title: 11. Settlement, Trade Conventions, and Disclosure
sections.overview: All standard debt securities now settle on a T+1 cycle (effective 5/28/2024) under SEC Rule 15c6-1 amendments and corresponding MSRB rule amendments. Knowledge of accrual conventions and required customer disclosures is essential.
key_concepts: T+1 regular-way settlement applies to: Treasuries (always T+1), corporate bonds (changed from T+2), municipal bonds (changed from T+2 effective 5/28/2024), standard ABS, and corporate equities.
Cash settlement: same-day; available by mutual agreement.
Accrued interest paid by buyer to seller from last coupon date up to but NOT including settlement date.
Corporate and muni accrued interest: 30/360 day-count convention (unchanged).
Treasury accrued interest: actual/actual day-count convention.
Trades 'flat' (without accrued interest): zero-coupon bonds, bonds in default, income bonds.
Confirmation requirements: trade confirmations must disclose capacity (agent/principal), markup/markdown where required, CUSIP, settlement date, accrued interest, yield.
rules: Rule 2261 — Disclosure of financial condition on customer request.
Rule 2262 — Disclosure of control relationship between member and issuer prior to transaction.
Rule G-17 — Fair dealing in municipal securities transactions.
Rule G-30 — Prevailing market price and reasonable markup/markdown standards for municipal transactions (waterfall analysis).
formulas: Settlement Date = Trade Date + 1 business day (regular way, T+1)
Accrued Interest = (Coupon Rate × Par × Days Accrued) / (360 [corp/muni] or 365/Actual [Treasury])
mnemonics: 'T+1 for All' — Treasuries, corporates, munis, ABS, equities (post-5/28/2024).
'Flat trades = Zero, Default, Income' (no accrued interest).
